title: The Change of Control Clause That Can Stall Your Sale After You've Already Agreed a Price
linkedin:
The price gets agreed. The term sheet gets signed. Then the buyer's lawyers start reading the lease, and a clause nobody has thought about in ten years becomes the thing the whole deal turns on.

We see this pattern often enough in exit work that it deserves a name: the change of control clause. It sits quietly in commercial leases, bank facilities, equipment finance agreements and key customer contracts, giving the other party the right to be asked, and sometimes the right to say no, before a business can change hands.

It is almost never found before due diligence. And due diligence happens after the price has already been agreed, which is exactly the moment the landlord or the key customer has the most leverage and the least reason to move quickly. A consent request can turn into a longer lease term, a rent increase, or renegotiated customer pricing, right when the seller has the least appetite to push back.

None of this is a flaw in how the business was run. It is a timing problem, and timing problems are solvable. Reading the assignment and change of control clauses in the handful of contracts that actually matter, the lease, the facility, the two or three biggest customer agreements, twelve months before going to market turns a mid negotiation surprise into a non event.

This is one of the eight dimensions a proper exit readiness review is built to check, alongside customer concentration and owner dependence, because a contract surprise unsettles a buyer's confidence in everything else they were told about the business.

If you're an Australian business owner who has started thinking about selling in the next few years, here's something worth checking now rather than later. Many commercial leases, bank facilities and major customer contracts include a clause requiring the landlord, lender or customer to consent before the business can change hands. These clauses are completely standard, and most of the time nobody even notices them, until a sale is actually underway and a buyer's lawyers start reading every contract line by line.

By then, the price has usually already been agreed, which is exactly the wrong time to discover that someone else holds a say over whether your deal can proceed. The businesses that avoid this surprise are the ones that read through their lease, loan and biggest customer contracts well before they ever go to market, and quietly deal with anything that needs attention.

It's a small bit of homework that saves a lot of stress later, and it's one of the areas we look at closely with business owners preparing for a future sale. Read the full piece on the blog.
